# Exercise 1. Forecasting with ARMA(1,1) and Parametric Bootstrap

**1.** Write a function `simulate_arma11` that takes as inputs starting values for $Y$ (`Y0`), $\varepsilon$ (`eps0`), the length of the series `N`, and parameters `phi`, `theta`, `sigma`, and returns a simulated series from an ARMA(1,1) process of length `N`. (Note that we use $T$ instead of $N$ in the lecture, but in R, `T` is reserved for `TRUE`.)

```{r ex1-simulate-function}
simulate_arma11 <- function(Y0, eps0, N, phi, theta, sigma){
  draws <- numeric(N + 1)
  shock <- numeric(N + 1)
  draws[1] <- Y0
  shock[1] <- eps0

  for (i in 1:N){
    m <- phi * draws[i] + theta * shock[i]          # conditional mean
    draws[i + 1] <- rnorm(1, mean = m, sd = sigma)  # new Y
    shock[i + 1] <- draws[i + 1] - m                # its shock
  }

  draws[-1]  # drop Y0, return the N simulated values
}
  

```

**2.** Use this function to generate a time series of length $N = 200$ from an ARMA(1,1) process with starting values $Y_0 = 0$ and $\varepsilon_0 = 0$ and parameters $\phi = 0.6$, $\theta = 0.3$, and innovation variance $\sigma^2 = 1$.

```{r ex1-generate-series}
sim <- simulate_arma11(Y0=0, eps0=0, N=200, phi=0.6, theta=0.3, sigma=1)
str(sim)
```

**3.** Split the data into a training set (70%) and a test set (30%).

```{r ex1-split}
n_train <- floor(0.7 * length(sim))

train <- sim[1:n_train]
test  <- sim[(n_train + 1):length(sim)]

H <- length(test)  # forecast horizon

```

**4.** Fit an ARMA(1,1) model on the training data.

```{r ex1-fit}
fit <- arima(train, order = c(1, 0, 1))
fit

```

**5.** Use the `simulate_arma11` function to generate forecasts (what are the starting values in this case?):

- Simulate $B = 500$ bootstrap sample paths from the fitted model for the test horizon.
- From these bootstrap forecasts, compute the mean forecast and the 90% prediction interval (5% and 95% quantiles).

> **Answer (starting values):**

```{r ex1-bootstrap}
B  <- 500
mu <- coef(fit)["intercept"]

# B bootstrap paths: rows = horizons (1..H), columns = paths
paths <- replicate(B, simulate_arma11(
  Y0    = tail(train, 1) - mu,
  eps0  = tail(residuals(fit), 1),
  N     = H,
  phi   = coef(fit)["ar1"],
  theta = coef(fit)["ma1"],
  sigma = sqrt(fit$sigma2)
) + mu)

# Summaries per horizon
mean_fc <- rowMeans(paths)
lower   <- apply(paths, 1, quantile, probs = 0.05)
upper   <- apply(paths, 1, quantile, probs = 0.95)



```

```{r echo=FALSE}
forecast_table <- data.frame(
  Horizon  = 1:H,
  Actual   = round(test, 3),
  Mean     = round(mean_fc, 3),
  Lower_5  = round(lower, 3),
  Upper_95 = round(upper, 3)
)

cat("Bootstrap forecasts (B =", B, "paths, 90% prediction interval)\n\n")
print(head(forecast_table, 10), row.names = FALSE)
cat("...\n")
cat(sprintf("\nShare of test points inside the 90%% interval: %.1f%%\n",
            100 * mean(test >= lower & test <= upper)))
```

**6.** Plot the results: training data, test data, bootstrap paths, mean forecast, and prediction interval.

```{r ex1-plot}
n      <- length(sim)
t_train <- 1:n_train
t_test  <- (n_train + 1):n

plot(sim, type = "n",
     ylim = range(sim, paths),
     xlab = "Time", ylab = "Y",
     main = "ARMA(1,1): bootstrap forecasts with 90% prediction interval")

# Bootstrap paths (light, transparent)
matlines(t_test, paths, col = adjustcolor("grey60", alpha.f = 0.08), lty = 1)

# Prediction interval as a shaded band
polygon(c(t_test, rev(t_test)), c(lower, rev(upper)),
        col = adjustcolor("steelblue", alpha.f = 0.25), border = NA)

# Data
lines(t_train, train, col = "black", lwd = 1.5)
lines(t_test,  test,  col = "darkorange", lwd = 1.5)

# Mean forecast and interval bounds
lines(t_test, mean_fc, col = "blue", lwd = 2)
lines(t_test, lower,   col = "steelblue", lty = 2)
lines(t_test, upper,   col = "steelblue", lty = 2)

abline(v = n_train + 0.5, lty = 3, col = "grey40")

legend("topleft", bty = "n", cex = 0.8,
       legend = c("Training data", "Test data", "Bootstrap paths",
                  "Mean forecast", "90% prediction interval"),
       col = c("black", "darkorange", "grey60", "blue", "steelblue"),
       lty = c(1, 1, 1, 1, 2), lwd = c(1.5, 1.5, 1, 2, 1))
```

**7.** Evaluate forecast accuracy:

- Compute the RMSE of the mean forecast and of the upper quantile forecast.
- Compute the quantile score for the mean forecast and for the upper quantile forecast.

```{r ex1-evaluate}
# Helper functions
rmse <- function(y, f) sqrt(mean((y - f)^2))

quantile_score <- function(y, q, alpha) {
  mean(ifelse(y < q, (alpha - 1) * (y - q), alpha * (y - q)))
}

alpha <- 0.95  # level of the upper quantile

# RMSE
rmse_mean  <- rmse(test, mean_fc)
rmse_upper <- rmse(test, upper)

# Quantile score (alpha = 0.95), averaged over the test horizon
qs_mean  <- quantile_score(test, mean_fc, alpha)
qs_upper <- quantile_score(test, upper,   alpha)

scores <- data.frame(
  Forecast       = c("Mean", "Upper quantile (95%)"),
  RMSE           = c(rmse_mean, rmse_upper),
  Quantile_score = c(qs_mean, qs_upper)
)
print(scores, row.names = FALSE, digits = 4)
```

# Exercise 2. Simulation Study: Effect of Model Misspecification

In this exercise, you will study how model misspecification impacts forecasting performance. You will conduct a Monte Carlo simulation where the data is generated from an autoregressive process of order 2 (AR(2)), while both AR(1) and AR(2) models are estimated and used to produce forecasts. The performance of these forecasts will then be evaluated and compared.

**1.** Generate a function `simulate_ar2` that takes as inputs starting values for $Y_1$ (`Y1`), $Y_0$ (`Y0`), the length of the series `N`, and parameters `phi1`, `phi2`, `sigma`, and returns a simulated series from an AR(2) process of length `N`.

```{r ex2-simulate-function}

simulate_ar2 <- function(Y1, Y0, N, phi1, phi2, sigma){
  y <- numeric(N + 2)
  y[1] <- Y0   # Y_0
  y[2] <- Y1   # Y_1 (most recent starting value)

  for (t in 3:(N + 2)){
    y[t] <- phi1 * y[t - 1] + phi2 * y[t - 2] + rnorm(1, mean = 0, sd = sigma)
  }

  y[-(1:2)]  # drop the two starting values, return N simulated values
}

```

**2.** Use this function to generate $B = 500$ independent replications of time series of length $N = 500$ from an AR(2) process with starting values $Y_1 = 0$, $Y_0 = 0$ and parameters $\phi_1 = 0.9$, $\phi_2 = -0.8$, and innovation standard deviation $\sigma_\varepsilon = 0.01$.

```{r ex2-generate-replications}

set.seed(123)

B <- 500
N <- 500

ar2_sims <- replicate(B, simulate_ar2(
  Y1    = 0,
  Y0    = 0,
  N     = N,
  phi1  = 0.9,
  phi2  = -0.8,
  sigma = 0.01
))

print(dim(ar2_sims))  # 500 x 500: rows = time, columns = replications
```

**3.** For each replication:

- Split the series into a training set (70%) and a test set (30%).
- Fit two competing models on the training set:
  - An AR(1) model.
  - An AR(2) model.
- Produce forecasts over the test horizon with both models, including the mean forecast and the 80% predicted quantile.
- Compute the following forecast evaluation metrics for each model:
  - Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE).
  - Mean Absolute Error (MAE).
  - Quantile score for the 80% predicted quantile, defined as
    $$  QS_\alpha\left(Y_{T+h}, \hat{Q}_{\alpha,T+h}\right) =
      \begin{cases}
      (\alpha - 1)\left(Y_{T+h} - \hat{Q}_{\alpha,T+h}\right) & \text{if } Y_{T+h} < \hat{Q}_{\alpha,T+h} \\
      \alpha\left(Y_{T+h} - \hat{Q}_{\alpha,T+h}\right) & \text{if } Y_{T+h} \geq \hat{Q}_{\alpha,T+h}
      \end{cases}
      $$ where $\alpha = 0.8$, $Y_{T+h}$ is the observed value at time $T+h$ and $\hat{Q}_{\alpha,T+h}$ is the forecasted quantile.
  - Average the quantile scores across the test horizon and define the mean quantile score as
    $$  \overline{QS}_\alpha = \frac{1}{H} \sum_{j=1}^{H} QS_\alpha\left(Y_{T+j}, \hat{Q}_{\alpha,T+j}\right),
      $$ where $H$ denotes the size of the evaluation (test) horizon.

```{r ex2-replication-loop}
mae <- function(y, f) mean(abs(y - f))
# rmse() and quantile_score() are reused from Exercise 1

alpha   <- 0.8
n_train <- floor(0.7 * N)
H       <- N - n_train

results <- data.frame(
  rep   = rep(1:B, each = 2),
  model = rep(c("AR(1)", "AR(2)"), times = B),
  RMSE  = NA, MAE = NA, QS = NA
)

for (b in 1:B) {
  y     <- ar2_sims[, b]
  train <- y[1:n_train]
  test  <- y[(n_train + 1):N]

  for (p in 1:2) {
    fit <- arima(train, order = c(p, 0, 0))
    fc  <- predict(fit, n.ahead = H)

    mean_fc <- as.numeric(fc$pred)
    q80     <- mean_fc + qnorm(alpha) * as.numeric(fc$se)  # 80% quantile

    row <- 2 * (b - 1) + p
    results$RMSE[row] <- rmse(test, mean_fc)
    results$MAE[row]  <- mae(test, mean_fc)
    results$QS[row]   <- quantile_score(test, q80, alpha)  # mean QS over H
  }
}


```

**4.** Collect the results (RMSE, MAE, $\overline{QS}_{0.8}$) from all $B$ replications for both models.

```{r ex2-collect-results}
head(results)
```

**5.** Compare the performance of AR(1) vs. AR(2) using boxplots for each metric:

- RMSE.
- MAE.
- Mean Quantile score.

```{r ex2-boxplots}
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))

boxplot(RMSE ~ model, data = results,
        main = "RMSE", ylab = "RMSE", xlab = "",
        col = c("tomato", "steelblue"))

boxplot(MAE ~ model, data = results,
        main = "MAE", ylab = "MAE", xlab = "",
        col = c("tomato", "steelblue"))

boxplot(QS ~ model, data = results,
        main = expression("Mean quantile score (" * alpha * " = 0.8)"),
        ylab = "Mean QS", xlab = "",
        col = c("tomato", "steelblue"))

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

# Average of each metric per model, for reference
aggregate(cbind(RMSE, MAE, QS) ~ model, data = results, FUN = mean)
```

**6.** Interpret the results and discuss how model misspecification (fitting AR(1) to AR(2) data) affects predictive performance.

> **Answer:**

The AR(2) does slightly better on all three metrics, but the gain is small relative to the variation across replications. With a 150-step horizon, both models’ forecasts quickly settle at the mean, so the AR(1)’s misspecification (it can’t capture the oscillation from φ₂ = −0.8) only costs accuracy at the first few horizons and gets diluted over the rest.
